lessons.title: History of Computers: Five Generations
lessons.notes_html:
The history of computers can be divided into five generations. The idea of the computer began with people who wanted an easier way to calculate numbers. With time, computers changed from huge, slow machines into the fast, intelligent machines we use today.

First and Second Generations

  • First generation (1942) — computers were huge in size, slow, unreliable and expensive. They used vacuum tubes. The ENIAC was 30 x 50 feet in size and 30 tons in weight.
  • Second generation (1955) — came with the invention of the transistor. Transistors were faster, more reliable, smaller and cheaper than vacuum tubes. Example: IBM 1401.

Third and Fourth Generations

  • Third generation (1964) — used Integrated Circuits (ICs), made of interconnected electronic components. They gave higher processing speeds, greater storage capacity and lower prices. Example: IBM 360 series.
  • Fourth generation — the modern computers we use nowadays. The microprocessor was introduced in this generation; these computers use very complex circuits on a microprocessor chip. Example: Apple I.

Fifth Generation

Fifth-generation computers are highly complex and are based on Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology. They are reliable, intelligent machines and include expert systems, game playing, robotics, natural language understanding and neural networks.

First1942 - 1955Vacuum tubeMachine and Assembly

Third1964 - 1975ICCOBOL, Fortran

Fifth1989 - PresentULSI circuitMercury, LISP, OPS5 and Prolog

Key Points

  • Computers developed through five generations.
  • Vacuum tubes, transistors, ICs, microprocessors and AI mark the five generations.
  • Each generation became smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable.

lessons.title: Systems: Natural and Artificial
lessons.notes_html:
A system is a collection of interconnected or interrelated components that work together to achieve a specific purpose. Any kind of system accepts input and produces output. Systems are of two main types: natural systems and artificial systems.

Natural Systems

Natural systems are parts of the natural world that function together as unified entities. They occur naturally in the environment without human creation or interference, and they operate independently of human involvement.

  • Ecosystems
  • Geological formations
  • The solar system
  • Weather patterns

Artificial Systems

Artificial systems are inspired by natural systems but are created by humans to serve specific objectives or goals. They are developed through deliberate planning and organization of components to achieve the desired results effectively.

  • Computer systems
  • Transportation networks
  • Communication systems
  • Healthcare systems

Key Points

  • A system is a set of connected parts working together for a purpose.
  • Natural systems exist in nature without human involvement.
  • Artificial systems are planned and created by humans for specific goals.

lessons.title: The Computer System: Hardware and Software
lessons.notes_html:
A computer system is a set of integrated devices that input, output, process and store data and information. Computer systems are built around at least one digital processing device. A computer system has two main components: hardware and software.

Hardware

Computer hardware consists of the physical parts of a computer. We can actually see and touch these components, such as the monitor, keyboard, mouse and hard disk.

Software

Computer software is a set of instructions that directs a computer to perform specific tasks or operations. Examples are Microsoft Windows, MS Word, media players and computer games.

HardwareSoftware
Tangible (physical) parts of a computer.Non-tangible parts of a computer.
Hardware is like the human body.Software is like the human soul.

Key Points

  • A computer system inputs, processes, outputs and stores data.
  • Hardware is what you can see and touch.

lessons.title: Input Unit and Input Devices
lessons.notes_html:
The devices which are used to input data and programs into the computer are known as the Input Unit. The input unit accepts instructions and data from the user, converts them into a computer-acceptable format and sends them to the computer system for processing. The hardware components of a computer are divided into five categories: input unit, processing unit, memory unit, output unit and storage unit.

Keyboard and Mouse

  • Keyboard — the most commonly used input device; data is entered by typing, like a typewriter. A standard keyboard has 101 keys: alphabet keys, number keys, function keys, navigation keys and a numeric keypad.
  • Mouse — a pointing device rolled over a mouse pad to control the cursor on the screen. It has two or three buttons and is used to click, double-click and drag.

Scanner, Microphone and Webcam

  • Scanner — enters information directly into the computer using a laser beam; it converts printed or written information, including photographs, into digital form. A hand-held scanner scans documents into digital forms that can be stored, edited, transferred and emailed.
  • Microphone — inputs voice, audio and sound; it converts human speech into electrical signals.
  • Webcam — a video camera designed to record or stream to a computer or network; used in video telephony, live streaming, social media and security.

Biometric Devices and Sensors

  • Biometric device — measures biological elements such as human features to log health/fitness data and authenticate users. Biometric data can be visual, audio, spatial and behavioral.
  • Digital sensor — produces data based on physical properties such as heat, light, pressure, moisture and motion.

Key Points

  • The input unit feeds data and programs into the computer in a form it can accept.
  • Keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone and webcam are input devices.
  • Sensors input data from the physical environment.

lessons.title: Inside the CPU: Control Unit, ALU, Registers and Buses
lessons.notes_html:
The main unit inside the computer is the Central Processing Unit (CPU). It is responsible for all events inside the computer, and all input and output devices connect with the system unit to work together. The microprocessor is the brain of the computer system; it consists of the Control Unit (CU) and the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU). A processor's speed is measured in Gigahertz (GHz) — the higher the speed, the faster the execution of instructions.

Control Unit and ALU

  • Control Unit (CU) — controls the operations of all parts of the computer and regulates their step-by-step working: Step 1 Fetch instruction, Step 2 Decode instruction into a command, Step 3 Execute command, Step 4 Store result in memory.
  • ALU — performs all arithmetic activities (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) through its Arithmetic Unit, and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT) through its Logic Unit, so the computer can make decisions and give answers in the form of True or False.

Registers

Registers are a type of computer memory built directly into the processor, used to store and manipulate data during the execution of instructions. A register may hold an instruction, a storage address or any kind of data.

RegisterFull NameFunction
MARMemory Address RegisterHolds the memory location of data that needs to be accessed.
MDRMemory Data RegisterHolds data being transferred to or from memory.
ACAccumulatorStores intermediate arithmetic and logic results.
PCProgram CounterContains the memory address of the next instruction to be executed.
CIRCurrent Instruction RegisterContains the current instruction during processing.

Buses

Buses are series of lines that connect the processor to other parts of the computer, such as cache memory or main memory.

BusFunction
Address BusCarries the addresses of data (but not the data) between the processor and memory.
Data BusCarries data between the processor, the memory unit and the input/output devices.
Control BusCarries control signals or commands from the CPU to control and coordinate all activities within the computer.

Key Points

  • The CPU is the brain of the computer; it consists of the CU and the ALU.
  • Registers are small, fast memories inside the processor.
  • Address, data and control buses connect the CPU with memory and devices.

lessons.title: Motherboard, Ports, Expansion Slots and Power Supply
lessons.notes_html:
The motherboard is the most essential part of a computer — the backbone of the computer system. All hardware devices are attached directly or indirectly with the motherboard.

Ports

Computer ports are physical connection interfaces on a computer where you can plug in external devices like keyboards, monitors, USB drives and printers. They are located on the motherboard, usually at the back of the system unit, and allow communication between the computer and peripheral devices. Examples are PS/2, serial, parallel, VGA, Ethernet and USB ports.

Expansion Slots

An expansion slot is a socket on the motherboard that can hold an expansion card. An expansion card (expansion board) is a small circuit board used to connect devices such as modems, sound cards, graphics cards and network interface cards to the computer.

  • PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) — the most common expansion slot in modern computers, used for sound cards, graphics cards and network cards; a motherboard typically has two to four PCI slots.
  • ISA (Industry Standard Architecture) — found only in Windows-based computers; operates at a much slower speed than PCI.
  • AGP (Accelerated Graphics Port) — a specialized slot used only for a graphics or video card; operates much faster than PCI.

Power Supply

The power supply is a critical component that converts electrical power from an external source (usually an AC wall outlet) into usable DC (Direct Current) power for the internal components of the computer. It also has built-in fans to prevent overheating.

Key Points

  • The motherboard connects all parts of the computer.
  • Ports connect external devices; expansion slots hold expansion cards.
  • The power supply converts AC power into DC power for the computer.

lessons.title: Memory Unit: RAM, ROM and Cache
lessons.notes_html:
The memory unit is used to store data and programs in a computer system. Data and instructions entered through input units must be stored inside the computer before actual processing starts. It is the working space of the computer.

RAM and ROM

  • RAM (Random Access Memory) — stores data and instructions currently being processed by the CPU. It is attached to the motherboard. Data in RAM is erased when the power is switched off, so RAM is called volatile memory or main memory. It is measured in megabytes (MB) or gigabytes (GB).
  • ROM (Read Only Memory) — a permanent, non-volatile memory. Once data is written onto ROM it cannot be removed, even when the computer is switched off. It contains the start-up instructions of the computer and information about its hardware devices, and is fixed on the motherboard.
ParameterRAMROM
VolatilityVolatile — contents are lost when the device is powered off.Non-volatile — contents are retained even if the device is powered off.
Read/WriteBoth read and write operations can be performed.The user can only read the information; it cannot be altered.
StorageStores temporary information.Stores permanent, non-erasable information.
Speed and CostFaster access speed; price is quite high.Slower speed; price is comparatively low.

Cache Memory

Cache memory stores frequently accessed information for a faster response time and improves system performance. It exists at three levels, each level getting progressively larger but slower than the one before: L1, L2 and L3. L1 cache is built inside the microprocessor, whereas L2 and L3 are on the motherboard. L1 cache is faster than L2 and L3 cache.

Key Points

  • RAM is volatile main memory for data being processed now.
  • ROM is permanent memory holding start-up instructions.
  • Cache memory keeps frequently used data close to the CPU for speed.

lessons.title: Storage Unit and Storage Devices
lessons.notes_html:
The storage unit provides space for storing data and information. Data and instructions are stored before processing, and the results produced by the computer are also kept in storage before being passed to the output units.

Hard Disk Drive and SSD

  • Hard Disk Drive (HDD) — a permanent storage device that stores a large amount of data compared to other storage devices. It contains several rotating disks called platters mounted on a central spindle, each with read/write heads, packed in an airtight metal case inside the system unit. Capacities range from 10 GB to 500 GB, 1 TB and 2 TB. It is reliable and durable.
  • Solid-State Drive (SSD) — a modern storage device that uses flash memory with no moving parts. It is faster than an HDD in booting, file transfers and overall responsiveness, and is more durable and shock-resistant, but usually more expensive for the same capacity.

Optical Discs and USB Flash

  • CD/DVD — flat, round plastic disks; portable and less expensive, but less reliable than a hard disk. A CD stores up to 700 MB and a DVD up to 4.7 GB. They are used to store data, software, games and movies.
  • USB flash drive — a portable, rewritable flash memory device that plugs into a USB port; also known as a Data Traveler. It is widely used to transfer data from one computer to another.
Storage TermApproximate Number of Bytes
Byte (B)1 byte (8 bits)
Kilobyte (KB)1 thousand
Megabyte (MB)1 million
Gigabyte (GB)1 billion
Terabyte (TB)1 trillion

Key Points

  • The HDD stores the largest amount of data on rotating platters.
  • SSDs use flash memory, are faster and have no moving parts.
  • CD, DVD and USB flash drives are portable storage devices.

lessons.title: Output Unit and Von Neumann Architecture
lessons.notes_html:
The output unit produces the final results of the computer in human-understandable form. It accepts the results produced by the computer, which are in coded form, and converts them into human-readable form.

Output Devices

  • Display screen — also called the Video Display Unit (VDU); displays text and graphics. By technology it is of three types: CRT (Cathode Ray Tube), LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) and LED (Light Emitting Diode).
  • Printer — transfers data from the computer onto paper. Types: dot matrix printers, inkjet printers and laser printers.
  • Plotter — draws large, high-quality images such as architectural blueprints, engineering designs and large posters; unlike printers, plotters draw continuous lines using pens. Types include drum, inkjet, flatbed and cutting plotters.
  • Speakers — produce digitized sound like music and audio.
  • Multimedia projector — displays the computer screen or output (text, image, video, audio) on a large screen or wall.

Von Neumann Architecture

The Von Neumann Architecture is a model of computer system design proposed by John von Neumann in 1945. It consists of a Control Unit, Arithmetic and Logic Unit, Memory Unit, Registers and Input/Output devices. It is based on the stored-program concept, where instructions and program data are stored in the same memory. It is the foundation of most modern computers.

Key Points

  • The output unit converts coded results into human-readable form.
  • Monitor, printer, plotter, speakers and projector are output devices.

lessons.title: System Software and the Operating System
lessons.notes_html:
Computer hardware cannot perform any task without software. Software is the set of instructions given to the computer to perform a specific task or operation. There are two main types of software: system software and application software.

System Software

System software directly operates the computer hardware, provides the basic functionality needed by users and other software, and provides a platform for running application software. It has four basic types: operating system, device drivers, utility programs and language translators.

Operating System

An operating system (OS) is system software responsible for managing the computer's hardware and software resources. Examples: DOS, Microsoft Windows (XP, Vista, 7, 8, 10, 11), Linux, Unix, Mac OS, Chrome OS, Android, Ubuntu and Solaris. Its important functions are:

  • Booting and user interface — loads the system files into RAM and provides a user interface so the user can work easily.
  • File management — lets the user create, save, delete, copy, paste and rename files and folders.
  • Managing programs — helps the user work with multiple programs at the same time; the active application is shown in the foreground and others in the background, and the user can switch using the task bar.
  • Device management — checks all devices at start-up and loads their drivers; when a new device is attached, it configures it and installs its driver.

Key Points

  • Software is the set of instructions that makes the computer perform tasks.
  • System software runs the hardware and provides a platform for applications.
  • The operating system manages hardware, files, programs and devices.

lessons.title: Device Drivers, Utility Programs and Language Translators
lessons.notes_html:
Device Drivers

A device driver is system software that controls a particular type of device and tells the operating system how to communicate with that device. A device cannot work properly if its driver is not installed — for example, the drivers of a printer, sound card or graphics card. Plug and Play (PnP) technology allows the operating system to automatically detect peripheral devices.

Utility Programs

A utility program is system software that performs a specific task related to the management of computer functions, resources or files. It allows a user to analyze, configure and maintain the computer. Examples: PC Doctor, antivirus, data recovery, backup, partition recovery and disk cleanup.

Language Translators

A language translator translates computer programs from a human-readable programming language into a machine-understandable language. Examples are compilers, interpreters and assemblers.

  • High-level language — easy for humans to read and write; uses English-like words and hides hardware details, e.g. Python, Java.
  • Low-level language — close to the computer's hardware; hard for humans to read but very fast for the computer, e.g. machine language (0s and 1s).
  • Assembly language — a low-level language that uses short words (codes) instead of 0s and 1s; easier than machine language but still close to hardware.

Key Points

  • A device driver lets the operating system communicate with a device.
  • Utility programs analyze, configure and maintain the computer.
  • Compilers, assemblers and interpreters translate programs into machine language.

lessons.notes_html:
Application software is a set of programs that enables the user to do a specific work on the computer. It has four main types.

Productivity Software

Productivity software is used to become more effective and efficient while performing daily activities. It facilitates office work, document management and collaboration. Popular examples are Microsoft Office Suite, Open Office, Libre Office and Google Workspace.

Business Software

Business software is designed to help companies perform various business functions efficiently, such as SAP (Systems, Applications and Products in Data Processing), QuickBooks, Google Workspace and Google Forms.

Entertainment Software

Entertainment software is developed to entertain users and is used for leisure activities, from media players to computer games. Examples are Spotify, Netflix and video games.

Educational Software

Educational software helps a user enhance learning and skill activities: Learning Management Systems (LMS), online encyclopedias and dictionaries, simulation programs, tutorials, Kahoot!, Duolingo, Google Classroom, Canva and Khan Academy. It helps students understand subjects through videos, practice exercises, quizzes and interactive activities, lets them study at their own pace, and gives instant feedback. A word processor such as Microsoft Word or Google Docs is used to type essays, assignments and reports, with editing, formatting and spell check. Canva is a design tool for posters, presentations, infographics and project covers.

Key Points

lessons.title: Programming Languages
lessons.notes_html:
Programming languages allow us to communicate with the computer. To perform a particular task, you write a program; a program written for a computer is known as software. There are hundreds of programming languages, from GWBASIC to Python, and each focuses on different types of tasks.

Categories by Use

BusinessCommercial, financial and administrative systems for data processing and enterprise software.COBOL, SQL, Visual Basic
EducationalDesigned for teaching programming concepts to beginners.Scratch, Logo, Python

Types by Paradigm

  • Procedural — a series of functions, instructions and statements run in a specific order; specifies how the computer solves a problem. Examples: BASIC, C, FORTRAN, Pascal.
  • Functional — created to manage processing and symbolic computing; its foundation is mathematics. Examples: Haskell, Erlang, Clojure.
  • Object-Oriented (OOP) — focuses software design on data, or objects, rather than functions and logic; an object is a data field with distinct attributes and behavior. Examples: C++, Java, Python.
  • Scripting — instructions written for a run-time environment; they do not require compilation and are interpreted instead. Examples: JavaScript, AWK, Perl.
  • Logic — program statements express facts and rules about problems within a system of formal logic. Examples: Prolog, Answer Set Programming (ASP), Datalog.

lessons.title: Hardware and Software Engineering
lessons.notes_html:
Hardware Engineering

Hardware engineering is the process of designing, developing, testing and manufacturing physical computer systems. Hardware engineers are detail-oriented and have in-depth knowledge of all physical components of a computer. Their typical duties include:

  • Creating models and prototypes of new systems.
  • Helping a company or organization update and repair computer systems.
  • Assembling and testing computer parts like circuit boards, chips and processors.
  • Presenting and explaining prototypes to managers, clients and fellow employees.
  • Working in a lab to run tests and analyze data.
  • Evaluating user needs and making relevant recommendations.
  • Troubleshooting processes related to computer hardware functionality.
  • Monitoring the production, installation and manufacturing of computer hardware systems.

Software Engineering

Software engineering is the process of creating, developing and testing computer programs such as online games, applications, network control systems and operating systems. Software engineers often work in teams, using creative and analytical skills. Their typical duties include:

  • Testing and monitoring a software program's performance.
  • Updating existing software systems.
  • Researching to develop more user-friendly programs.
  • Overseeing the implementation of new system software.
  • Training new users and explaining how to operate software.
  • Collaborating with other software engineers and developers.
  • Drawing and outlining software diagrams and models for developers to code.
  • Collecting and analyzing data to track software performance and plan future updates.

Key Points

  • Hardware engineering designs and manufactures physical computer systems.
  • Software engineering creates, develops and tests computer programs.

lessons.title: Computer Networks and Their Types
lessons.notes_html:
A computer network is when two or more computers are connected to share information and resources like files and the internet. In a network, all data is sent using only two numbers: 0 and 1 — the binary system. Computers use 0 and 1 because they work with electrical signals that have two states: 1 means ON and 0 means OFF. Text, pictures and videos are changed into 0s and 1s, travel through cables or wireless connections, and are changed back at the other device. The internet is the global communication network that allows almost all computers worldwide to connect and exchange information.

LAN, MAN and WAN

  • LAN (Local Area Network) — connects a group of systems and devices within a limited geographical area, such as a building or adjacent buildings. Most LANs connect personal computers and devices including printers, and a LAN is usually owned by one organization.
  • MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) — larger than a LAN; covers several buildings and offices in the same city and can connect two or more LANs. A cable television network in a city is a good example.
  • WAN (Wide Area Network) — a very large network covering a state, province, country or the whole world. It interconnects LANs and MANs. The internet is the best example of a WAN.

VPN

A Virtual Private Network (VPN) is a mechanism for creating a secure connection between a computing device and a computer network, or between two networks, using an insecure communication medium such as the public internet.

Key Points

  • A network connects computers to share information and resources.
  • Data travels in binary: 1 is ON and 0 is OFF.
  • LAN is limited to a building, MAN covers a city, and WAN can cover the world.

lessons.title: Wireless Networks
lessons.notes_html:
A wireless network allows devices like phones, laptops and tablets to connect and communicate with each other without using physical cables. Instead of wires, it uses radio waves or infrared signals to send data.

Advantages of Wireless Networks

  • Mobility and flexibility — devices can connect from anywhere within range and users can move without losing connection.
  • Easy installation — no need to run cables through walls or ceilings; quick setup, especially in homes and temporary setups.
  • Cost-effective — saves money on cabling and physical infrastructure.
  • Supports multiple devices — many users can connect to the same network at the same time.

Disadvantages of Wireless Networks

  • Slower speeds compared to wired networks, especially with many users.
  • Signal interference — walls, metal objects or other electronic devices can weaken or block signals.
  • Limited range — the farther you are from the router, the weaker the signal.
  • Security risks — easier to hack if not secured properly; encryption like WPA2/WPA3 and strong passwords are needed.

Key Points

  • Wireless networks use radio waves or infrared instead of cables.
  • They give mobility and easy setup but have limited range and security risks.

Wi-Fi and Cellular

  • Wi-Fi (Wireless Fidelity) — allows computers, smartphones, tablets and other devices to connect to the internet or to each other without wires, through radio waves. Widely used in homes, offices, airports and public places. Advantages: high data transfer speed, supports many devices, no physical cables. Disadvantages: limited coverage area, security risks if not protected, performance decreases with many users.
  • Cellular communication — a radio network distributed over land through cells, each with a fixed-location transceiver called a base station. Together the cells provide coverage over large areas, so mobile phones can communicate even while moving through cells. Advantages: wide coverage, supports voice and data, high mobility. Disadvantages: requires SIM and service plan, congestion can slow speed, signal strength varies by location.

Satellite and GPS

  • Satellite communication — satellites provide telecommunication links between different places across the globe; used for TV distribution, broadcasting live matches, long-distance telephone communication and communication with ships and aircraft. Advantages: covers large and remote areas, useful for global broadcasting, reliable for long distances. Disadvantages: high cost, signal delay (latency), affected by bad weather.
  • GPS (Global Positioning System) — a network of orbiting satellites that send details of their position in space back to Earth; GPS receivers calculate the exact position, speed and time at the vehicle's location. It is freely available to anyone with a GPS receiver. Advantages: accurate location tracking, works worldwide, free to use. Disadvantages: does not work well indoors, requires a clear view of the sky, consumes battery power.

Bluetooth and NFC

  • Bluetooth — an open wireless technology standard for transmitting data over short distances between fixed and mobile devices; it creates personal networks. Used by MP3 players, mobile and peripheral devices, handheld computers and laptops. Its operating range depends on the device class.
  • NFC (Near Field Communication) — a short-range wireless technology that lets devices exchange data when they are very close, about 4 cm, using radio waves at 13.56 MHz. Used for contactless payments, ID cards, ticketing and quick data sharing. Active devices both generate signals; passive devices have only one signal-generating device. Advantages: very secure due to short range, fast connection without pairing, low power consumption. Disadvantages: very short range, low data transfer speed, limited to close-contact applications.

Key Points

  • Wi-Fi connects devices locally; cellular networks cover wide areas through cells.
  • Satellites and GPS work over the whole globe.
  • Bluetooth and NFC are short-range technologies; NFC works within about 4 cm.

lessons.title: Network Architecture and Communication Basics
lessons.notes_html:
Network architecture is the design or layout of how computers and other devices are connected and communicate in a network. It defines how data flows, how resources are shared and how devices interact with each other.

Client-Server Architecture

In client-server architecture, client devices request services or resources and a central server provides them. This model is the foundation of most modern networks, including the internet. A server is a computer that serves data to other computers and users. A client is the device that sends requests and receives responses from the server.

Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Network

In a peer-to-peer network, all computers (called peers) have equal status. Each computer can act as both a client (requesting resources) and a server (providing resources). There is no central server; for example, any of three connected computers can send or receive files directly from the other two.

Components of a Computer Network

  • Sender — the person or entity initiating the communication, e.g. your smartphone or laptop.
  • Receiver — the person or entity who receives the sent message, e.g. your friend's smartphone.
  • Message — the information the sender wishes to share, e.g. text, image or voice note.
  • Protocol — a set of rules that determines how data will be transmitted over the network, e.g. TCP/IP, HTTPS.
  • Transmission media — the medium through which data is transferred, e.g. Wi-Fi or mobile data. Physical media use wires and cables like fiber optic and coaxial cable; wireless media use unguided media like infrared waves, electromagnetic waves and microwaves.

Key Points

  • In client-server networks a central server provides services to clients.
  • In P2P networks all peers are equal and share directly.
  • Sender, receiver, message, protocol and transmission media make communication possible.

lessons.title: Modes of Communication and Switching
lessons.notes_html:
Modes of data communication are the methods used to communicate data between devices in a network. There are three modes: simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex.

Simplex, Half-Duplex and Full-Duplex

  • Simplex mode — communication is unidirectional, like a one-way street. Only one device can send and the other can only receive; the entire channel capacity is used in one direction. Example: the keyboard (input only) and the monitor (output only).
  • Half-duplex mode — each station can send and receive, but not at the same time. Example: a walkie-talkie, in which messages are sent one at a time in both directions.
  • Full-duplex mode — data is transmitted in both directions simultaneously; the channel capacity is divided between the two directions. Example: a telephone network, where both people can talk and listen at the same time.

Synchronous and Asynchronous Transmission

  • Synchronous transmission — carries a frequent stream of data in the form of signals along with timing signals generated by an electric clock, which keeps the sender and receiver synchronized. Data is transmitted in blocks or frames at specific times.
  • Asynchronous transmission — works on start and stop bits; each character contains its start and stop bit, with an irregular interval of time between characters.

Packet Switching and Circuit Switching

  • Packet switching — data is broken into small packets; each packet is sent independently over the network, packets may take different paths, and they are reassembled at the destination. Example: the internet and emails.
  • Circuit switching — a dedicated communication path is established between two devices for the entire duration of the communication; a complete path is reserved before communication starts and all data travels along that fixed path. It is reliable and consistent, with no delay once the circuit is established. Example: traditional telephone calls.

Key Points

  • Simplex is one-way, half-duplex is both ways in turn, full-duplex is both ways at once.
  • Packet switching sends independent packets; circuit switching reserves a fixed path.

lessons.title: Communication Devices and Network Topologies
lessons.notes_html:
Communication devices are hardware components used to send and receive data between computers or other electronic systems.

Communication Devices

  • Switch — allows computers in a network to connect with one another using wired communication; it uses packet switching to receive and forward data to the destination device.
  • Router — forwards data packets between computer networks and selects the best route.
  • Bridge — connects two or more different LANs that have a similar protocol and provides communication between the devices in them; joining multiple LANs multiplies the capacity of a single LAN.
  • Wireless Access Point (WAP) — allows wireless-capable devices to connect to a wired network.
  • DSL modem — runs over standard telephone lines and connects to the computer with a network card; in a DSL connection the telephone line remains free to make calls, and it is a high-speed method of accessing the internet.

Types of Connection

  • Point-to-point connection — allows one device to communicate with one other device, e.g. two phones pairing to exchange contacts or pictures.
  • Multipoint connection — two or more devices use the same communication line to send and receive data; many devices share one link.

Network Topologies

Network topology is the arrangement of a network, comprising nodes and connecting lines via sender and receiver.

TopologyHow It WorksAdvantagesDisadvantages
BusAll devices connect to a single central cable (the bus); data travels in both directions along the cable.Easy to set up; requires less cable.If the main cable fails, the entire network goes down; slower as more devices are added.
StarAll devices connect to a central device like a switch or hub; data passes through the central point.Easy to manage and add new devices; failure of one device does not affect the rest.Depends on the central device; more cable is needed.
RingDevices are cabled in a circular loop, the last device connecting to the first; data travels in one direction (or two in a dual ring).Data flows at a constant speed; good for small networks.Failure of one device can affect the whole network; difficult to troubleshoot.
MeshEach device is directly connected to every other device, offering multiple paths for data.Very reliable due to multiple paths; if one link fails, data finds another route.Expensive and complex to set up; uses a lot of cabling.

Key Points

  • Switches, routers, bridges, WAPs and DSL modems connect networks and devices.
  • Bus, star, ring and mesh are the basic network topologies.
  • Star is the most commonly used topology.

lessons.title: The OSI Model and Encapsulation
lessons.notes_html:
The OSI model was developed in the late 1970s and officially published in 1984 by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), to provide a standard framework allowing different computer systems and networking technologies to communicate with each other. It is like a step-by-step guide that shows how computers talk to each other over a network. It has seven layers, and each layer has a job to do. The model makes it easier to find and fix network problems, check how secure the network is, and talk about network attacks. A layer is a discrete set of functions the protocol is designed to accomplish.

Functions of the OSI Layers

No.LayerFunction
1Physical LayerDeals with hardware e.g. cables, switches, voltages; sends bits (0s and 1s).
2Data Link LayerEnsures reliable point-to-point data transfer; adds MAC addresses; handles error detection.
3Network LayerFinds the best path for data; handles IP addresses and routing.
4Transport LayerBreaks data into segments; ensures reliable delivery; uses TCP (reliable) and UDP (faster, less reliable) protocols.
5Session LayerStarts, manages and ends communication sessions.
6Presentation LayerFormats data, e.g. encryption, compression, encoding.
7Application LayerProvides services for user applications like email and web browsing.

Think of sending a letter: the Application layer is writing the message, Presentation is translating it into another language, Session is starting the conversation with a greeting, Transport is splitting the message into envelopes, Network is choosing the best delivery route, Data Link is putting the address on each envelope, and Physical is mailing the letter physically.

Encapsulation

Encapsulation is the process of wrapping data with necessary protocol information before it is transmitted over a network. It happens at each layer of the OSI or TCP/IP model, where each layer adds its own header (and sometimes trailer) to the data. Encapsulation always takes place at the sender's side. Data becomes a segment at the Transport layer, a packet at the Network layer, a frame at the Data Link layer, and finally bits (0s and 1s) at the Physical layer.

Key Points

  • The OSI model has seven layers, from Physical (layer 1) to Application (layer 7).
  • It was published by ISO in 1984 as a standard reference model.
  • Encapsulation wraps data with headers at each layer on the sender's side.

lessons.title: Protocols and the Internet
lessons.notes_html:
A data communication protocol is a mechanism or set of procedures that enables devices to communicate back and forth across the internet. To communicate together, two devices must support the same protocol, or a gateway is used to translate the communication.

Key Protocols

  • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) — makes sure data is sent and received accurately; it breaks data into packets, sends them one by one and checks that all arrive safely; if any packet is lost, it sends it again.
  • IP (Internet Protocol) — finds the correct address for where data should go; every device on a network has a unique IP address.
  • HTTP/HTTPS — the language web browsers use to talk to websites, to request and receive web pages, images and other content.
  • DNS (Domain Name System) — translates domain names (www.google.com) into IP addresses (142.250.190.14) so your device can connect to the correct server.
  • DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) — automatically assigns an IP address and other settings, like gateway and DNS server, to devices when they connect to a network.
  • FTP (File Transfer Protocol) — used to send and receive files between computers on a network, e.g. uploading files to a website.
  • SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — used to send emails from one computer to another, like a mailman delivering your email to the right email server.

The Internet and How It Works

The Internet is a huge network of computers all over the world connected to each other. It began as ARPANET: in January 1969, ARPA started an experimental computer network connecting universities; in the 1980s the National Science Foundation (NSF) and private companies developed the technologies that became known as the Internet. Vinton Gray Cerf, co-designer of the TCP/IP protocol, is recognized as the father of the Internet. When you use the internet: your device connects through Wi-Fi, mobile data (4G/5G) or a wired Ethernet connection provided by an ISP; you request information by typing a website address; the request is broken into packets that travel through cables, routers and servers in many hops to the web server; the server sends the data back in packets, which your device reassembles; and protocols like TCP/IP ensure correct delivery while HTTPS keeps data safe with encryption.

Advantages of the Internet

  • Easy access to information and self-learning through search engines like Google.
  • Simple communication, online education (YouTube, Khan Academy, Coursera) and e-commerce (Amazon, Daraz, eBay).
  • Entertainment (Netflix, YouTube, Spotify), online banking and bill payments, and remote work.
  • Global awareness through real-time news, social networking (Facebook, Instagram, X) and cloud storage (Google Drive, Dropbox).

Key Points

  • Protocols are the rules that let devices communicate; TCP/IP runs the internet.
  • DNS turns names into IP addresses; DHCP assigns addresses automatically.
  • The internet grew out of ARPANET (1969) and connects millions of devices worldwide.

lessons.title: Problems and Identifying a Computing Problem
lessons.notes_html:
A problem is an obstacle, challenge, difficulty, task, or any other circumstance that needs to be resolved. Problems exist across all sectors, including education, healthcare, economics, transportation and commerce.

Area / SectorProblem
EducationMany students do not have access to quality education or learning resources.
HealthcarePeople in remote areas often struggle to get proper medical care.
EconomicsUnemployment makes it hard for people to earn a living and support their families.

Identifying a Computing Problem

Identifying a computing problem means recognizing a task or issue that can be solved using a computer or technology. It is the first step in problem-solving, where we try to understand what the problem is and why it needs to be solved. We ask:

  • What is the problem?
  • Can this problem be solved with a computer?
  • Who is facing the problem?
  • What is the goal, or what needs to be improved?

Examples: Students forget homework deadlines — can we create a reminder app or system to help them? A shopkeeper has trouble keeping track of daily sales — can we make a program to record and calculate sales?

Key Points

  • A problem is any obstacle or task that needs to be resolved.
  • A computing problem is one that can be solved using a computer.
  • Identifying the problem clearly is the first step of problem-solving.

lessons.title: The Six-Step Problem Solving Process
lessons.notes_html:
In computer science, a computing problem is a problem that is solved step-by-step using computation. Such problems usually have a well-defined input and desired properties that the output must satisfy. For solving a problem, a six-step process is used, and these steps are followed in sequence.

The Six Steps

  • 1. Identify the problem — the first and most important step: understand and clearly define the problem and establish a precise problem statement. Example: the printer is not working — is it turned on? Is it out of paper or ink?
  • 2. Decompose the problem — break the big problem into smaller, more manageable parts. Techniques include abstraction, mind mapping, divide and conquer, refinement and modularization. Example: is the printer connected properly? Is there power? Is there paper or ink? Is the computer sending the print command?
  • 3. Generate potential solutions — analyze the problem from more than one perspective and list all possible solutions, e.g. check the power cable, refill paper or ink, restart the printer, reconnect the USB or Wi-Fi, reinstall the printer driver.
  • 4. Select and design the ideal solution — compare the advantages and disadvantages of the potential solutions and select the best one, keeping in view the constraints. Ask: Is it safe? Is it simple? Will it solve the root problem?
  • 5. Implement the solution — turn the ideal solution into actions. Success depends on how well you identified and represented the problem.
  • 6. Evaluate the solution — after implementation, seek feedback and validate the solution. Example: after plugging in the printer, try printing again; if it works, the problem is solved — if not, try the next solution.

Key Points

  • The six steps are: identify, decompose, generate, select, implement, evaluate.
  • Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, easier parts.
  • Evaluation checks whether the solution actually worked.

lessons.title: Computational Thinking: Four Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Computational thinking is the process of identifying a clear, defined, step-by-step solution to a complex problem by thinking like a computer scientist. It includes breaking down a problem into smaller pieces, recognizing patterns and eliminating extraneous details, so that the step-by-step solution can be replicated by humans or computers. It trains your brain to think clearly, logically and creatively.

The Four Properties

  • Decomposition — breaking down a big problem into smaller, more manageable parts.
  • Pattern recognition — looking for things that repeat or are similar in different situations; it helps to predict what will happen next and speeds up problem-solving.
  • Abstraction — focusing only on important details and ignoring the unimportant ones; it helps you concentrate on the main idea of a problem.
  • Algorithmic thinking — creating a set of steps (called an algorithm) to solve a problem; it makes solutions repeatable and efficient, and they can be coded into a computer.

Example: A Slow Computer

  • Decomposition — Is it slow at the power-on step? Does it take long after logging in? Are programs loading slowly?
  • Pattern recognition — Does this happen every time you start it? Does it happen only when many apps are installed?
  • Abstraction — Ignore things like desktop wallpaper or sounds; focus on system start-up and app loading.
  • Algorithmic thinking — Step 1: Check how many apps open at start-up. Step 2: Remove unwanted start-up programs. Step 3: Scan for viruses. Step 4: Restart and observe the speed.

Key Points

  • Computational thinking solves complex problems step by step.
  • Its four properties are decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithmic thinking.

lessons.title: Logical and Algorithmic Thinking
lessons.notes_html:
Logical Thinking

Logical thinking means using clear, step-by-step reasoning to solve problems or make decisions. You gather facts, look for clues, and reach a conclusion that makes sense. It is always based on evidence, reasoning and facts. It involves reasoning, analysis, deductive logic, inductive logic and clarity of thought. Example: You feel cold in a room. Is the fan or AC on? Yes. Is the window open? Yes. If the window is open, cold air is coming in — therefore, close the window. Facts + reasoning = logical thinking.

Algorithmic Thinking

An algorithm is a sequence of steps to solve a problem in a precise and systematic way. Algorithmic thinking is the process used when creating the ordered steps of an algorithm. Algorithms are generally written in plain English. Once a successful solution to a problem has been found, it can be used repeatedly for the same problem — for example, calculating the mean of a set of numbers is always the same: add up all the numbers and divide the total by how many numbers are in the set.

Benefits of Algorithmic Thinking

  • An algorithm uses a definite procedure.
  • It is easy to understand because it is a step-wise representation of a solution.
  • It is independent — not dependent on any language.
  • Every step has its own logical sequence.
  • It is easy to find and remove errors.

Key Points

  • Logical thinking reaches conclusions from facts and reasoning.
  • Algorithmic thinking creates ordered steps that can be reused.

lessons.title: Algorithms: Properties and Writing
lessons.notes_html:
After fully understanding the problem, the next step is to plan a solution. The word algorithm is derived from the name of the mathematician Mohammed ibn-Musa al-Khwarizmi. An algorithm is a detailed step-by-step instruction set or formula for solving a problem or completing a task — a sequence of numbered steps.

Purpose of Algorithms

Writing the algorithm of a program before starting coding is a very beneficial habit in computer programming. It resolves various errors and confusion, and algorithms help the programmer write code faster by following the steps in the algorithm.

Six Properties of an Algorithm

PropertyMeaning
InputData to be processed.
OutputResulting information.
DefinitenessThe sequence of steps is clear and precise.
EffectivenessEach step is doable / possible.
FinitenessThe algorithm must stop eventually.
GeneralityThe algorithm applies to a set of inputs.

Writing an Effective Algorithm

  • Obtain complete information of the problem.
  • Analyze the problem.
  • Think of a problem-solving approach.
  • Develop a basic algorithm.
  • Improve and refine the algorithm.

Example — algorithm to print the sum of all given numbers: Step 1: Start. Step 2: Initialize sum = 0. Step 3: Input the total count of numbers, say n. Step 4: Repeat for i = 1 to n: input number x, add x to sum. Step 5: Print sum. Step 6: End.

Key Points

  • An algorithm is a numbered, step-by-step solution written before coding.
  • Every algorithm must have input, output, definiteness, effectiveness, finiteness and generality.

lessons.title: Flowcharts, Pseudocode and Concept Maps
lessons.notes_html:
Flowcharts

A flowchart is a diagram that shows the steps of a process using different symbols connected by arrows. It gives a step-by-step solution to a problem and shows the input, process and output. It helps in understanding the logic of the problem-solving process, gives a pictorial representation of the process, and shows the flow in a sequential manner.

ShapeNameFunction
OvalStart / EndRepresents a start or end point.
Arrow (line)ConnectorShows the logical flow between the shapes.
ParallelogramInput / OutputRepresents input or output.
RectangleProcessRepresents a process.
DiamondDecisionIndicates a decision.

Guidelines: a flowchart should be clear, neat and easy to follow; use standard symbols; the flow is either from left to right or from top to bottom; only one flow line should enter a decision symbol, but two flow lines may come out, one for each possible answer; only one flow line is used in the Start/End symbol. Popular flowchart tools are Microsoft Visio, Lucidchart, SmartDraw and EdrawMax.

Pseudocode

Pseudocode is a method of describing a process, or writing programming code and algorithms, using natural language. It is not the code itself, but a description of what the code should do. Example — area of a square: Step 1: Get the length of one side. Step 2: Multiply the length by itself. Step 3: Store the result in a variable called area. Step 4: Display the area. While writing pseudocode: follow the sequence of tasks, write a statement that determines the goal, use if-else like in the main code, and use proper casing — lowercase for variables, camel case for methods, uppercase for constants.

Concept Maps

A concept map is a visual diagram that shows relationships between ideas. It helps you organize and connect your thoughts clearly, and is very useful for planning essays or projects. Its parts are: concepts (main ideas or topics), links (lines or arrows that show relationships) and connecting words (which explain how ideas are related).

Key Points

  • A flowchart pictures an algorithm with standard symbols and arrows.
  • Pseudocode describes an algorithm in natural language.
  • A concept map connects ideas with links and connecting words.

The Web, also known as the World Wide Web (WWW), is a system of sharing information using the internet. It allows people to access websites, read articles, watch videos and connect with others through web browsers like Chrome, Firefox or Safari. A webpage is a single page that you see on the internet; it can contain text, images, videos, links and other multimedia. Every time you click a link or type a Uniform Resource Locator (URL), it opens a webpage. A website is a collection of related webpages connected under one web address (URL); all its webpages share the same domain name. For example, www.wikipedia.org is a website containing thousands of webpages.

Web Applications

A web application is a type of software or program that runs in a web browser. You do not need to download or install it; you use it just by visiting a website through the internet. How a web application works: you open a browser and go to the web app's URL; the browser sends a request to the server; the server processes your request and sends back the result; the result is shown on your screen as an interactive webpage.

A web developer is a person who builds and maintains websites and web applications: designing how a website works, writing code, making sure the website works on phones, tablets and computers, and fixing bugs and updating websites. lessons.title: HTML Basics and the DOM
lessons.notes_html:
HTML stands for Hyper Text Markup Language. It is the basic building block of all websites and is used to create the structure of web pages. HTML tells the web browser what content to display on the page and how it is arranged. It does not style the page or make it interactive — that is the job of CSS and JavaScript — but it provides the foundation.

A Simple HTML Page

<!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head> <title>My First Website</title> </head> <body> <h1>Welcome to My Website</h1> <p>This is a paragraph of text.</p> <img src="image.jpg" alt="Sample Image"> <a href="https://example.com">Visit Example</a> </body> </html>

To write HTML code, open a text editor such as Notepad, Visual Studio Code or Sublime Text, and save your file with a .html extension. Double-click the HTML file and your default web browser opens it and renders the page.

FeatureDescription
TagsHTML uses tags like <h1>, <p> and <img> to define elements.
StructureOrganizes content into sections like headings, paragraphs and images.
Static ContentHTML creates static content, which does not change unless the code is edited.

Installing Visual Studio Code

Visual Studio Code is the most popular code editor and IDE provided by Microsoft for writing programs in different languages. To install it on Windows: visit the official website, press the Download for Windows button, open the downloaded installer, complete the installation, and the Visual Studio Code window opens — now you can create a new file and begin your web development journey.

The HTML DOM

The HTML Document Object Model (DOM) is a tree-like structure that represents the content of a web page in a way that web browsers can understand and developers can interact with using code. When a web page is loaded, the browser reads the HTML and turns it into a DOM tree; each part of the HTML (headings, paragraphs, images) becomes a node or object in this tree.

Key Points

  • HTML structures web pages with tags; CSS styles them and JavaScript makes them interactive.
  • HTML files are saved with the .html extension and opened in a browser.
  • The DOM is the tree of nodes the browser builds from your HTML.

lessons.title: CSS: Styling Web Pages
lessons.notes_html:
CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It is a language used to style and design web pages created with HTML. While HTML gives structure, CSS controls how that structure looks — colors, fonts, layout, spacing and more. CSS lets you style everything in a separate file and merge the CSS on top of the HTML, which makes the HTML markup simpler and easier to manage. Without CSS, websites would look plain and unorganized.

Three Types of CSS

  • Inline CSS — styling written inside an element's style attribute, e.g. <p style="color:red;">Text</p>. Each component must be styled one by one, so it is not the most efficient approach, but it is useful to change a single element or quickly preview changes.
  • Internal / Embedded CSS — styles written inside a <style> tag in the <head> of the HTML file, e.g. <style> p { color: red; } </style>. The styles load every time the page is refreshed and cannot be used on multiple pages, but everything stays on one page, which makes sharing a preview simpler.
  • External CSS — all styling is handled in a separate .css file, written in any text editor and saved with a .css extension; the file should not contain HTML elements. It is applied to any page with a <link> tag inside the head section: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. External styling can improve loading times.

Key Points

  • CSS controls colors, fonts, layout and spacing of a web page.
  • Inline CSS styles one element; internal CSS styles one page; external CSS styles many pages from one file.

lessons.title: JavaScript Basics: Variables and Operators
lessons.notes_html:
JavaScript is a programming language used in web development to make websites interactive, dynamic and functional. While HTML provides the structure and CSS handles the design, JavaScript brings the website to life by allowing user interactions and real-time updates — clicking a button, filling out a form, showing or hiding content, displaying pop-up messages, and creating slideshows or animations. In HTML, JavaScript code is inserted between <script> and </script> tags. With JavaScript you can change HTML content (for example, document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML) and change HTML attribute values, such as the src of an image to turn a bulb on and off.

Variables

A variable is an entity that stores a value for later use. Variables in JavaScript are containers used to store data values like numbers, text (strings) or other types, and they give the data a name. Rules for naming variables: must begin with a letter, $ or _; cannot start with a number; are case-sensitive (name and Name are different); use camelCase (e.g. userName, totalMarks). There are three ways to declare variables:

  • var — the oldest keyword; function-scoped, but not recommended in modern JavaScript because it can lead to confusing behavior.
  • let — the most commonly used today; stores a value that can be changed later and is block-scoped. Example: let age = 16;
  • const — also block-scoped, used for a value that should not change during the program. Example: const pi = 3.14;

You can also declare a variable without an initial value, like let score; and assign a value later.

Operators

Operators are special symbols or keywords used to perform operations on values and variables — calculations, decisions and control of the program flow.

Operator TypeDescriptionExamples
Arithmetic OperatorsPerform basic math operations.+ , - , * , / , %
Assignment OperatorsAssign values to variables.= , += , -= , *= , /=
Comparison OperatorsCompare two values and return true or false.== , === , != , < , >
Logical OperatorsCombine or invert conditions.&& (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)

Key Points

  • JavaScript makes web pages interactive and dynamic.
  • Variables are declared with var, let or const; let and const are block-scoped.
  • Operators perform arithmetic, assignment, comparison and logical operations.

lessons.title: JavaScript Control Structures: Conditions and Loops
lessons.notes_html:
Conditional Statements

Conditional statements are used to make decisions in a program based on certain conditions. They allow the code to perform different actions depending on whether a condition is true or false, making a website react to different inputs and situations.

StatementDescriptionExample Use
ifRuns a block of code only if the condition is true.if (score > 50) { console.log("Pass"); }
elseRuns a block of code if the if condition is false.else { console.log("Fail"); }
else ifChecks another condition if the previous if was false.else if (score === 50) { ... }
switchChecks many possible values for a variable.switch (grade) { case 'A': ... }

Example: a time-based greeting — if the time is less than 15, the greeting is "Good Morning"; else if less than 20, "Good Day"; else "Good Evening".

Iterative Statements (Loops)

Iterative statements, also called loops, repeat a block of code multiple times as long as a specific condition is true, so you do not have to write the same code again and again.

Loop TypeDescriptionExample Use
forRepeats code a specific number of times.Count from 1 to 10.
whileRepeats code while a condition is true.Keep running until a value is reached.
do...whileRuns code at least once, then checks the condition.User input until correct.

Nested Loops

Nested loops place one loop inside another loop. The inner loop runs completely each time the outer loop runs once. They are powerful for handling complex data structures and repeated patterns, especially tasks involving rows and columns — for example, printing a star pattern of five rows.

Key Points

  • if, else, else if and switch make decisions in code.
  • for, while and do...while loops repeat code.

Arrays

An array in JavaScript is a special variable used to store multiple values in a single container. Instead of creating separate variables for each value, you can group them together. Arrays can hold numbers, strings, objects or even other arrays, and are used widely in loops, conditions and functions. Example: const Subjects = []; Subjects[0] = "Urdu"; Subjects[1] = "English"; Subjects[2] = "Mathematics"; — and a for loop can print every value stored in the array.

Functions

A function in JavaScript is a block of reusable code designed to perform a specific task. Functions make programs more organized, modular and efficient, because the same code can be executed many times without rewriting it. Example: function myFunction(p1, p2) { return p1 * p2; } — calling myFunction(4, 3) returns 12. Code written inside a function can be tested by calling the function and checking its return value.

A complete simple webpage combines all three technologies: HTML for structure, CSS for styling and JavaScript for interactivity. lessons.title: Debugging and the Console
lessons.notes_html:
Debugging is the process of finding and fixing errors (bugs) in your code to make sure it runs correctly. Bugs can cause a website or web application to behave unexpectedly, and debugging helps you identify the exact problem and correct it.

Type of ErrorDescription
Syntax ErrorMistyped code or missing symbols (e.g. a missing bracket).
Reference ErrorTrying to use a variable that does not exist.
Type ErrorUsing a value in the wrong way (e.g. calling a number like a function).
Logic ErrorCode runs without crashing, but gives wrong results.

The console.log() Method

Use console.log() to trace values, read error messages carefully, test small parts of code separately, and use breakpoints to pause and inspect code. lessons.notes_html:
Data science is an interdisciplinary field that uses scientific methods, algorithms, processes and systems to extract knowledge and insights from structured and unstructured data. It combines elements of statistics, computer science, machine learning and domain expertise (business knowledge) to turn raw data into actionable information. Its key objective is to extract useful information for strategic decision making, product creation, trend analysis and forecasting.

Scope of Data Science

  • Data analysis and visualization — exploring patterns and trends using graphs, charts and statistical summaries.

lessons.title: Data and Types of Data
lessons.notes_html:
Data refers to raw facts, figures or symbols that represent information about objects, events or concepts. It can be in the form of numbers, text, images, audio or video, and by itself it may not have meaning until it is processed or analyzed. Data is described as "the fuel" for driving businesses in the proper direction. Mainly, data is classified into two types: quantitative data and qualitative data.

Quantitative Data

Quantitative data is numerical and measurable information that can be used to identify trends, relationships and make predictions. It is further classified as:

  • Discrete data — countable, individualized figures that exist only in discrete increments and cannot be divided further, e.g. number of tickets, number of customers. Bar graphs, line charts, histograms and pie charts are used to represent it.
  • Continuous data — numerical data representing the unspecified number of measurements between two realistic points, e.g. height, weight (pounds), temperature, time and cost.

Qualitative Data

Qualitative data gathers and interprets non-numerical facts; it describes attributes and characteristics. It is collected by questionnaires, interviews or observation and is typically presented in narrative form. It is divided into:

  • Nominal data — categorizes data by labeling or naming values, such as gender, hair color or types of animals. It has no hierarchy.
  • Ordinal data — classifies data based on rank, such as social standing (wealthy, middle income, poor) or education level. There are no fixed intervals between the categories.

Key Points

  • Data is raw facts and figures; it gains meaning when processed.
  • Quantitative data is numerical: discrete (countable) or continuous (measurable).
  • Qualitative data describes attributes: nominal (names) or ordinal (ranks).

lessons.title: Datasets, Databases and the Fields Behind Data Science
lessons.notes_html:
Datasets and Databases

A dataset is a collection of related data, generally in the form of a table or spreadsheet, that is primarily used for analysis. In the relational model, a table is a relation, each row (also called a record, tuple or observation) represents one entry or instance, and each column (also called a field or attribute) represents a specific variable or feature about the entries. A database is used to store and manage data, while data science focuses on analyzing, modeling and drawing insights from that data. For example, a bank database stores customer details, transaction history and loan records, while data science analyzes this data to detect fraud, predict loan default or segment customers.

The Fields Behind Data Science

  • Computer science — the study of computers and computational systems, covering software development and design, the algorithms that make up software, and how software interacts with hardware.
  • Statistics — one of the core pillars of data science, providing the methods and tools to collect, analyze, interpret and present data; it forms the mathematical foundation of data science.
  • Mathematics — the backbone of data science; it enables data scientists to make sense of data, build models and draw reliable conclusions.
  • Artificial intelligence (AI) — the simulation of human intelligence in machines programmed to think and act like humans. Data science prepares and processes the data that AI systems need to learn and make decisions.
  • Machine learning — a field of AI that allows systems to learn and optimize operations without being repeatedly programmed; it uses data, statistics, mathematical models and trial and error to learn a task.
  • Deep learning — a field of machine learning that relies on artificial neural network design: layers of interconnected nodes called neurons that process and learn from input data. In machine learning, feature extraction and classification are separate steps; in deep learning they are combined.
  • Data mining — the process of identifying and analyzing massive amounts of raw data to discover patterns and extract relevant information; companies use it to understand customers, create better marketing strategies, boost sales and cut costs.

Business Knowledge

Adding data science to business operations can improve productivity, decision-making and product creation. Its key benefits are: better business decisions from objective information; measuring performance through data collection and patterns; increasing efficiency of everyday operations; mitigating risk and fraud, as machine learning algorithms can detect fraud from a user's regular behavior; and enhancing customer experiences by learning customers' preferences and dislikes.

Key Points

  • A dataset is a table of records (rows) and attributes (columns).
  • Databases store and manage data; data science analyzes it.
  • Statistics and mathematics are the foundation; AI, machine learning and deep learning build on data.

Data collection is the process of gathering information from all the relevant sources to find a solution to the research problem. It helps to evaluate the outcome of the problem, and the data collection methods allow a person to conclude an answer to the relevant question. Data collection is of two types: primary and secondary.

Primary Data Collection

  • Interview method
  • Questionnaire method
  • Schedules
  • Surveys
  • IoT devices
  • Sensors

Secondary Data Collection

  • Government records
  • Websites

lessons.notes_html:
Data Visualization

Data visualization is the graphical representation of information and data. Its main goal is to make it easier to identify patterns, trends and outliers in large data sets. The term is often used interchangeably with information graphics, information visualization and statistical graphics. When a data scientist is developing complex predictive analytics or machine learning algorithms, it is critical to be able to see the outputs, to monitor results and confirm that the models are working as expected.

Data Storage

Data storage refers to the retention of digital information on recording media, so that it can be accessed by computers or other devices for future use. It makes it easy to back up files for safekeeping and quick recovery in the event of an unexpected computing crash or cyber attack. Data can be recorded and stored in three main forms:

  • File storage — data is stored in files and folders, organized in a hierarchy; this is how data is stored on computer hard drives or cloud storage such as Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive.
  • Block storage — data is split into evenly sized blocks, stored separately along with the identifiers needed to locate them; often used in cloud storage or Storage Area Networks (SANs), so blocks can be found and accessed quickly.
  • Object storage — an architecture designed to handle large amounts of unstructured data, such as email, videos, photos or web pages — anything that cannot be organized into a traditional relational database.

Key Points

  • Visualization shows patterns, trends and outliers in pictures and charts.
  • Data is stored as files, blocks or objects.

lessons.title: Big Data
lessons.notes_html:
Big data refers to data that is so large, fast or complex that it is difficult or impossible to process using traditional methods. This data can be non-relational, like tweets, photos or videos, or relational, like databases or Excel sheets. Examples of big data tools are Tableau, Apache Hadoop (free), Bluemix of IBM and Zoho Analytics.

The Three Vs of Big Data

  • Volume — organizations collect data from transactions, smart (IoT) devices, industrial equipment, videos, images, audio, social media and more. Cheaper storage using data lakes, Hadoop and the cloud has eased the burden of storing it all.
  • Velocity — with the growth of the Internet of Things (IoT), data streams into businesses at an unprecedented speed and must be handled in a timely manner; RFID tags, sensors and smart meters drive the need to deal with these torrents of data in near-real time.
  • Variety — data comes in all types of formats, from structured, numeric data in traditional databases to unstructured text documents, emails, videos, audios, stock ticker data and financial transactions.

Big data management and processing strategies are part of data science: data is collected to perform analysis on it, and since not all patterns can be identified with statistical analysis, machine learning is often used to identify patterns from data.

Applications of Big Data

  • Government — optimize public services, enhance decision-making, address social issues, and predict and prevent crime.
  • Education — personalized learning by analyzing student performance, attendance and engagement.
  • Healthcare — digitized patient records, medical history, test results, treatment plans and even genetic data.
  • Telecommunication and multimedia — main users of big data, handling large-scale data generated every day.
  • E-commerce — vast amounts of customer data, including browsing history, purchase behavior and preferences.

Key Points

  • Big data is too large, fast or complex for traditional processing methods.
  • Its three Vs are volume, velocity and variety.
  • Big data is used in government, education, healthcare, telecom and e-commerce.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a broad branch of computer science concerned with building smart machines capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence. It is the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines, especially computer systems. Specific applications of AI include expert systems, natural language processing, speech recognition and machine vision. Artificial intelligence (AI) creates machines that can think, learn and decide, much like people do. AI is being used more and more in fields like healthcare, finance and self-driving cars. Its advantages include accuracy (fewer errors), efficiency (tasks are done faster), automation (repetitive jobs are automated), and the ability to process large volumes of data.

Machine Learning

Machine learning (ML) is a field of artificial intelligence that uses statistical techniques to give computer systems the ability to "learn" (progressively improve performance on a specific task) from data, without being explicitly programmed. It helps in predictive analysis and decision making. Machine learning is divided into three categories:

  • Supervised learning — the algorithm is trained on labeled data, meaning the input-output pairs are known.
  • Unsupervised learning — the algorithm works with unlabeled data and tries to find hidden patterns or structures.
  • Reinforcement learning — an agent learns to make decisions by performing actions and receiving feedback (rewards or penalties) from the environment.

Key Points

  • AI builds machines that perform tasks needing human intelligence.
  • ML lets computers learn from data without explicit programming.
  • ML has three categories: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning.

Supervised Learning

In supervised learning, the algorithm is trained on labeled data — the input-output pairs are known. The goal is to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs so the model can predict outputs for new, unseen data. Types of supervised learning:

  • Classification — predicts categorical labels, e.g. spam or not spam emails.
  • Regression — predicts continuous values, e.g. predicting house prices.

Applications of supervised learning: spam detection in emails, image classification, medical diagnosis, sentiment analysis, credit scoring and speech recognition.

Unsupervised Learning

In unsupervised learning, the algorithm works with unlabeled data and tries to find hidden patterns or structures. There is no explicit feedback or correct output provided during training. Types of unsupervised learning:

  • Clustering — groups similar data points together, e.g. customer segmentation.
  • Association — finds rules that describe large portions of data, e.g. market basket analysis (people who buy bread also buy butter).
  • Dimensionality reduction — reduces the number of random variables under consideration, e.g. Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

Applications of unsupervised learning: customer segmentation, anomaly detection, data compression, recommendation systems, topic modeling and market basket analysis.

Key Points

  • Supervised learning uses labeled data: classification predicts labels, regression predicts values.
  • Unsupervised learning finds hidden patterns in unlabeled data: clustering, association, dimensionality reduction.

lessons.title: Areas of AI: Speech, Vision, NLP and Expert Systems
lessons.notes_html:
To understand the areas and capabilities of artificial intelligence, it is important to look closely at each area of work:

  • Speech recognition — also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition, or speech-to-text; it enables a program to process human speech into a written format. While it is commonly confused with voice recognition, speech recognition focuses on the translation of speech from a verbal format to a text format, whereas voice recognition just seeks to identify an individual user's voice.
  • Computer vision — a field of AI that enables computers and systems to derive meaningful information from digital images, videos and other visual inputs — and take actions or make recommendations based on that information. If AI enables computers to think, computer vision enables them to see, observe and understand. It works much the same as human vision, except humans have a head start: human sight has the advantage of lifetimes of context to train how to tell objects apart, how far away they are, whether they are moving, and whether there is something wrong with an image.
  • Natural language processing (NLP) — a subfield of computer science, artificial intelligence and linguistics concerned with the interactions between computers and human languages, particularly how to program computers to process and analyze large amounts of natural language data. NLP is a way for computers to analyze, understand and derive meaning from human language in a smart and useful way.
  • Expert systems — a computer system that emulates the decision-making ability of a human expert. They are designed to solve complex problems by reasoning through bodies of knowledge, represented mainly as if-then rules, rather than through conventional procedural code.

Benefits of AI

Key benefits of artificial intelligence include: increased efficiency and automation, improved decision-making, enhanced accuracy, personalized user experience, cost reduction and better problem solving.

Key Points

  • Speech recognition turns speech into text; voice recognition identifies a user's voice.
  • Computer vision lets machines see, observe and understand images.
  • Expert systems reason with if-then rules like a human expert.
